botin.name: Restaurante Sobrino de Botín (Casa Botín)

history.fact: Botín opened in 1725. Guinness World Records lists it under the record title "Oldest restaurant" (holder: Restaurante Botín, Madrid, 1725).
A second Guinness page, "Oldest operating restaurant," names Casa Botín (1725) and says it has run without a break since it opened.
The restaurant says the 1987 Guinness Book of Records was the edition that first named it the oldest restaurant in the world.
Records show the building existed by 1590.

A French cook, Jean Botín, came to Madrid with his Asturian wife. In 1725 her nephew, Cándido Remis, opened a small inn on Calle Cuchilleros. That is where the name "Sobrino de Botín" (Botín's nephew) comes from.
Until well into the 1700s, inns could not sell meat or wine. They could only cook what the traveler brought in.
The González family took over in the 20th century. During the Civil War it served as a dining hall for militiamen. After the war, the sons Antonio and José built it into what it is now.
The wood-fired oven has been in use since the restaurant opened. It burns holm oak. The restaurant calls it the soul of the house.
Suckling pigs and lambs from the Segovia area arrive three or four times a week.
The restaurant has four floors. It has kept its old inn feel through many renovations.
In 2025 another Madrid tavern, Casa Pedro, said it dates from 1702 and challenged Botín's title. That date had not been proven at the time of the report.

famous_diners.name: Ernest Hemingway
famous_diners.story: At the end of The Sun Also Rises (Spanish title Fiesta, 1926), Jake and Brett eat roast suckling pig with rioja alta in Botín's upstairs dining room. Jake calls it "one of the best restaurants in the world." Hemingway mentions Botín's suckling pig again in Death in the Afternoon (1932).

famous_diners.name: Francisco de Goya
famous_diners.story: Said to have worked here as a teenager in 1765. The restaurant says the 1987 Guinness edition calls him a dishwasher. Many retellings call him a waiter. Treat it as legend.

famous_diners.name: Martin Luther King Jr.
famous_diners.story: Michael Aaron Rockland, a former US cultural attaché, writes in A Diplomat in Franco's Spain (2011) that he took King to dinner at Botín.

famous_diners.name: James A. Michener
famous_diners.story: The American novelist wrote about eating at Botín, "just off the Plaza Mayor."

famous_diners.name: Graham Greene and Frederick Forsyth
famous_diners.story: Both put Botín in their novels: Greene in Monsignor Quixote (1982) and Forsyth in Icon, which Botín's site calls "The Black Manifesto" (1996). Forsyth sets a scene in the brick-arched cellar.

famous_diners.name: Benito Pérez Galdós
famous_diners.story: The novelist is named among Botín's famous guests.

famous_diners.name: Spanish royal family
famous_diners.story: Visited in 2011 and ate the same dishes as everyone else.

botin.rooms: Four floors. The ground floor has the entrance, the old oven and the kitchen. The upstairs rooms have tiled floors, period furniture and old paintings; two of them are the Castilla and Felipe IV rooms. Hemingway's characters ate upstairs. The basement cellar (the cueva) has old brick arches and once held the wine. It is small, dim and tight, and it has alcoves. Some diners love it, and people who don't like tight spaces may not.

specialties.notes: The house signature. The piglet is from Segovia and is roasted in the wood oven. The skin should be crisp and the meat soft. The price is for one serving.
The second roast. It comes from the same oven, Castilian style.

specialties.dish: Sopa de ajo con huevo y jamón (garlic soup with egg and ham)
specialties.notes: Classic Castilian starter. It contains ham.
A house specialty from the fish side of the menu.

specialties.dish: Tarta Botín ("Booty" cake: sponge cake and cream)

reservations.lead_time: Not found. Botín does not say how far ahead it fills up. Reviewers say last-minute tables are hard to get, so book as soon as possible.
reservations.notes: Book online through the form on Botín's website, which runs on TheFork. If your time is full, the site says you can usually still book online at 1:00 pm or 11:15 pm on any day, except on special dates. To change the number of diners, call +34 91 366 42 17 or email botin@restaurantebotin.com. Check your spam folder for the confirmation email. Walk-ins sometimes work if you line up when lunch starts at 1:00 pm, but you can't pick your room.

tips: When you book, ask for the cellar (cueva) if you want the old brick vaults. Ask for an upstairs room if you want more light and more space.
If you walk in, line up before 1:00 pm. Walk-ins usually can't pick the cellar or the top floor.
At a late dinner, desserts may have run out. An earlier time gives you more choice.
Plan on two hours or more. The meal is slow.
Each cochinillo or lamb order is one person's serving (€32.50 or €33.00). For two people, order one each, or share one roast plus starters. The roasts come with potatoes.
One reviewer says a modest dinner for two can stay under €100, but plan to spend more with wine.
Want to see the oven and cellar up close? Botín sells its own "Botín Secrets Route" tour with dinner.
botin.dress: Not found. Botín publishes no dress code.
botin.vegetarian: There is no vegetarian section on the menu, and most vegetable dishes come with Iberian ham. Dishes on the menu with no meat listed: asparagus with mayonnaise (€15.50), gazpacho (€12.50), scrambled eggs with wild asparagus (€14.50), pure sheep cheese (€15.50) and Russian salad (€14.00). Russian salad in Spain often has tuna, so ask. Desserts include Catalan cream, rice pudding, cheesecake and sorbet (€7.50–€9.50). Ask staff about broths and fats.

how_its_made.fact: A cochinillo is a very young piglet that has drunk only its mother's milk. The "Cochinillo de Segovia" label requires this.
Under the Segovia guarantee label, piglets are at most three weeks old. They weigh 4.5–6.5 kg alive and 3.8–5.8 kg when sold.
Los Galayos in Madrid says its Segovia piglets are no older than 21 days and weigh 4.5–5 kg at most.
In 2024 the EU registered "Cochinillo de Segovia" as a protected geographical indication (IGP).
The Segovia recipe is very simple. The pig is roasted whole in a wood oven with only water and salt. This makes the skin golden and crisp.
Segovia cooks use only water and salt, while many other countries marinate or stuff the pig.
It is roasted in a clay dish in a brick wood oven. Cooks watch the color and add or pull back wood. They say it comes down to experience, not a fixed recipe.

Plate-cutting: at Mesón de Cándido in Segovia, the pig is cut with the edge of a plate to show how tender it is. Then the plate is thrown to the floor and smashed. The house says Cándido López started the custom.
Casa Duque in Segovia says its family was already cutting cochinillo with a plate around 1880, a habit passed down from Julián Duque.
One story says the first Cándido had no knife at hand, used a plate, and dropped it by accident. The bones are soft enough that a plate cuts clean where a knife can stick.
At Botín the oven burns holm oak and has been lit since the house opened.

similar.name: Casa Lucio
similar.signature: Huevos estrellados (broken fried eggs over fries). Roast suckling pig is also on the menu.
similar.hours: Every day. Lunch 1:00–4:00 pm, dinner 8:00–11:30 pm. Closed in August.
similar.why_go: A La Latina classic famous for its broken eggs. It also serves roast suckling pig, so you get both in one meal.
similar.notes: Book by phone (+34 91 365 82 17), by WhatsApp (+34 608 400 171), or by email for groups of 12 or more. There is no online booking form. Bread is €2.50 a person.

similar.name: Posada de la Villa
similar.signature: Cuarto de cordero asado en horno de leña (quarter roast lamb from the wood oven)
similar.price: Not found. The website lists dishes without prices.
similar.hours: 12:45–3:45 pm and 7:45–11:30 pm. Closed Sunday night.
similar.why_go: An inn from 1642 on Cava Baja, restored in 1980 as a roasting house. It is known for wood-oven lamb. Cocido is also available if you order ahead.
similar.notes: No roast suckling pig on the menu, only lamb. Closed Sunday night (Nov 1). Phone +34 91 366 18 60, or email reservas@posadadelavilla.com.

similar.name: Los Galayos
similar.signature: Cochinillo lechón asado (roast suckling pig, roasted about 8 hours)
similar.hours: Every day. Restaurant noon to midnight. Kitchen 11:30 am to 11:30 pm with no break.
similar.why_go: Right on Plaza Mayor, a short walk from Botín. The pigs come from Segovia with the guarantee label. The kitchen never closes in the afternoon, so it's an easy backup.
similar.notes: Open since 1894. The bar does not take bookings. The restaurant does not take bookings by email, and it holds a table for 15 minutes.

similar.name: El Landó
similar.signature: Huevos estrellados (sister house of Casa Lucio); cochinillo frito (cochifrito) and paletilla de cordero (lamb shoulder)
similar.price: Huevos estrellados €14.00; cochifrito €25.50; paletilla de cordero €31.50
similar.hours: Tuesday–Saturday: lunch 1:00–4:00 pm, dinner 8:30–11:45 pm. Sunday lunch only, 1:00–4:00 pm. Closed Sunday night and all day Monday.
similar.why_go: Owned by Lucio Blázquez of Casa Lucio. It has the same famous eggs in a quieter setting by the Vistillas gardens, with views of the Almudena Cathedral.
similar.notes: It does not serve roast suckling pig, only fried pig (cochifrito). The menu does not say whether the lamb shoulder is roasted. Closed Sunday night (Nov 1). Phone 913 66 76 81; WhatsApp +34 682 010 232.

similar.name: Mesón de Cándido
similar.signature: Cochinillo asado al estilo Cándido, cut with a plate that is then smashed
similar.price: Not found. The online menu loads in a viewer that could not be read.
similar.hours: Every day. Lunch 1:00–4:30 pm, dinner 8:00–11:00 pm.
similar.why_go: It sits at the foot of the Roman aqueduct. This is the house that made Segovia cochinillo famous, and it still does the plate-cutting and plate-smashing show.
similar.notes: Other house dishes: judiones de La Granja (big white beans), roast lamb and ponche segoviano for dessert. Phone +34 921 425 911.

similar.name: Restaurante José María
similar.address: Calle Cronista Lecea 11, 40001 Segovia (next to Plaza Mayor)
similar.signature: Cochinillo asado from the house's own farm (Cochinillo de Segovia IGP)
similar.price: Cochinillo €34.00; roast lamb (a quarter, for two) €78.50; tasting menus €63 and €78 per person
similar.hours: Kitchen: Sunday–Thursday noon–10:30 pm; Friday–Saturday noon–11:00 pm. Bar from 10:00 am.
similar.why_go: A favorite with locals since 1982. It raises its own piglets on its own farm. It has a lively tapas bar, and the menu marks vegetarian dishes, which helps a mixed table.
similar.notes: Autumn 2026 menu. Bread is €2.00 a person. Phone +34 921 461 111. The kitchen serves all afternoon with no break.

similar.name: Casa Duque
similar.signature: Cochinillo asado from a 100-year-old wood oven; quarter roast suckling lamb for two
similar.price: Cochinillo €32.00 a serving; quarter lamb for two €70.00; set menu (starters, cochinillo, ponche cake, wine, coffee) €50 per person
similar.hours: Not found on the official site.
similar.why_go: Opened in 1895. It calls itself Segovia's oldest restaurant, and the fourth and fifth generations of the family run it. It sits on the walking street between the aqueduct and Plaza Mayor.
similar.notes: Phone +34 921 46 24 87. Grilled seasonal vegetables cost €17. Bread is €1.10.

segovia_trip.train: High-speed train (Renfe Avant, AVE, Avlo, or OUIGO) from Madrid Chamartín to Segovia Guiomar station.
segovia_trip.time: About 25–30 minutes on the fastest trains. About 30 direct trains a day, from about 6:15 am to 11:30 pm.
segovia_trip.cost: Fares change with the time and how early you book. One guide gives Avant fares from €19.70. Omio lists fares from about €7–9 up to about €46, with an average of about €20–24 each way.
segovia_trip.notes: Guiomar station is about 7 km from the old town. City bus line 11 goes to the aqueduct in about 15 minutes for about €2. A slower option is the bus from Madrid's Moncloa station, about 1 hour 20 minutes, from about €4.16. Check times and fares on renfe.com before you go.
